query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In-situ interface doping, which promotes dopant segregation to the internal lamellar boundaries of the eutectic high-entropy alloy, will enhance interfacial bonding and toughness, thereby simultaneously increasing the strength and room-temperature tensile ductility compared to the unmodified alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy exhibiting a dual-phase lamellar colony microstructure (fcc/B2 or similar) with numerous internal boundaries prone to microcrack initiation.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor, in-situ doping element during alloy processing that preferentially segregates to the lamellar interfaces.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile deformation under otherwise identical casting/processing conditions, where the dopant concentration is optimized to modify only the interfaces without destabilizing the dual-phase structure.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced interfacial bonding via dopant segregation that increases the cohesion and toughness of the lamellar colony boundaries.
generation.mechanism: By doping the interfaces, the local bonding strength is increased and the interface becomes tougher, which delays or prevents microcrack nucleation and propagation under tensile load. This improved load transfer across lamellar colonies allows simultaneous improvements in both yield strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: The doped alloy will exhibit higher yield and ultimate tensile strengths and a higher tensile ductility at room temperature relative to the baseline undoped eutectic alloy, with a delay in the onset of microcracking observed via microstructural analysis.
generation.baseline: The untreated eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies, which under conventional processing shows a strength–ductility trade-off and early microcracking at internal boundaries.
generation.boundary: The intervention is applicable only when the dopant concentration is moderate enough to segregate at the interfaces without altering the bulk phase stability or the overall lamellar morphology. Its beneficial effects are expected under room-temperature loading conditions and may not extend to elevated temperatures.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal choice and concentration of the dopant, as well as the long-term stability of the doped interfaces under cyclic or variable loading conditions, remain to be experimentally determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same eutectic high-entropy alloy composition. One set is processed with the in-situ interface doping intervention while the other set is processed by standard methods (baseline). Conduct identical room-temperature tensile tests and perform electron microscopic examinations to monitor the structural integrity and dopant distribution at the interfaces.
measurements: Tensile stress–strain curves to extract yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and ductility (% elongation)
High-resolution TEM to map dopant segregation at the lamellar interfaces
Fractography to identify the origin and propagation of microcracks
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the doped samples fail to exhibit a statistically significant simultaneous increase in both strength and ductility compared to the baseline, or if TEM analysis shows that the interface doping does not lead to enhanced interfacial bonding (evidenced by persistent or worsened microcrack initiation at the boundaries), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High-performance refractory alloys with ultrahigh strength and ductility are in demand for a wide range of critical applications, such as plasma-facing components. However, it remains challenging to increase the strength of these alloys without seriously compromising their tensile ductility. Here, we put forward a strategy to “defeat” this trade-off in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys by stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs). The coherent interfaces of SCCPs facilitate the dislocation transmission and relieve the stress concentrations that can lead to premature crack initiation. As a consequence, our alloy displays an ultrahigh strength of 2.15 GPa with a tensile ductility of 15% at ambient temperature, with a high yield strength of 1.05 GPa at 800 °C. The SCCPs design concept may afford a means to develop a wide range of ultrahigh-strength metallic materials by providing a pathway for alloy design. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical engineering

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.
